passes.title: Retail autopilot drone with tag and phone
passes.note: Every part a first complete build would want, priced from retail. This is the starting point for every reduction.

passes.title: Used autopilot, Pi Zero streams video, ground station runs detection
passes.note: A used autopilot saves some of the flight-controller cost. The Pi Zero streams video, and a phone or laptop on the ground runs detection. Risk added: control now depends on the ground link, so the autopilot's own link-loss failsafe must be tested in simulation. The close-range ToF is dropped until logs show a need.

passes.title: Printed frame and guards
passes.note: Printed structure replaces the commercial frame. Risk added: printed parts fail differently from moulded ones, so every printed load-bearing part needs a bench stress test before flight.

passes.title: Bench-first kit (no flying drone yet)
passes.note: Buy only what the bench rig needs: a Pi Zero, a camera, the tag, and printed parts. Sensors and companions are tested on a desk and the replay tool gets real logs. The flying parts wait until those logs justify them. The Tello is optional for indoor follow-logic tests.

passes.title: Used feature-rich phone replaces the Pi and camera on the drone (example)
passes.note: An example of a used phone as the drone's computer and camera. The Pixel was bought for $250, far more than the Pi and camera it replaces. It buys GNSS, IMU, camera and compute. Risk added: about 188 g of extra weight, a phone battery on a drone (fire and crash risk), and a MAVLink bridge to the autopilot that must be built and tested.

passes.title: Bench kit with a made tag: bulk ESP32-C3 and outsourced board
passes.note: Replaces the retail HT-CT62 with a bulk ESP32-C3 module and an outsourced 2-layer board. The ESP32's Wi-Fi replaces the LoRa chip, since the drone's access point is within follow distance. Risk added: Wi-Fi range and dropouts must be measured in the field before this is trusted. The saving is small, because the GNSS module and antenna dominate the tag cost.

passes.title: Printed structure with DIY motor research and a thrust stand
passes.note: Replaces the four retail motors with DIY outrunners, and adds a thrust stand to measure them. Risk added: DIY motors may be less efficient or less reliable than the retail motor. Measure thrust per watt before using them on a drone. Magnets bought per disc are the largest cost.

passes.title: Owned pipeline: printed structure, made tag, DIY motor research
passes.note: Combines the printed structure, the made tag, DIY motor research and the thrust stand. Still bought: the autopilot, GPS, ESC, transmitter, battery, charger and props. The patch antenna is an unverified design on a bought board. The mill is optional capital, and FAU or IEEE may already have one.

passes.title: Own most: made autopilot board, ESC, transmitter and tag battery
passes.note: Replaces the bought autopilot board, ESC, transmitter and tag battery with designs made from chips and outsourced or printed parts. Not costed: the autopilot firmware port, the barometer, magnetometer and regulators, and the ESC MOSFET prices (placeholders). Each made design needs bench tests and a review before use. The receiver stays bought for now.

passes.title: Own most, with the by-weight and salvage motor target
passes.note: What-if pass: the motors use magnets bought by weight, and wire and shaft salvaged. This is only real after a magnet quote and a salvage check. Compare it with pass 8 to see the value of those two routes.

passes.title: Closer to the factory: factory-assembled boards, factory magnets and bearings, lab-etched stators
passes.note: The owner's board designs are assembled by the PCB factory from its own parts stock. Magnets and bearings come from factories at their minimum orders. Stator laminations are photo-etched in the lab (unverified). The tag moves to a BLE chip and a clone GNSS module (both untested). An allowance covers import duty, since small parcels from China no longer enter duty-free. Risk added: minimum orders tie up cash, duty rates are uncertain, and every new part needs a test before it replaces a proven one.

passes.title: Factory stator cores at a 1,000-piece minimum
passes.note: What-if pass: stator cores from a factory instead of the lab. Per unit it is close to the lab route, but the minimum order needs about $1,000 to $2,000 of cash up front, plus a drawing and 10 to 12 weeks of tooling. Only sensible as a group order.
